think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 65-year-old woman undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (pembrolizumab) for metastatic melanoma presents with new-onset hemoptysis and an enlarging right upper lobe solitary pulmonary nodule on CT. The central diagnostic challenge is differentiating malignant melanoma lung metastasis or immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced pneumonitis from activated pulmonary tuberculosis unmasked by immune checkpoint inhibition in an immunocompromised/immunomodulated oncology patient.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs when the patient presents in February 2017 with hemoptysis, and chest CT shows enlargement of the right upper lobe lesion without lymphadenopathy or effusion, prior to flexible bronchoscopy, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing, transbronchial biopsy, and mycobacterial culture.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pulmonary metastatic melanoma progression was the leading oncologic suspicion for an enlarging lung nodule and hemoptysis, but transbronchial biopsy showed caseous necrosis without melanoma tumor cells, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing was positive. Immune-checkpoint inhibitor-induced pneumonitis (an immune-related adverse event) was considered given concurrent autoimmune manifestations (vitiligo, sicca symptoms, positive anti-RO52 antibodies), but CT showed a focal consolidating lesion rather than diffuse interstitial/ground-glass changes, and tissue biopsy confirmed mycobacterial necrosis. The diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis is confirmed by positive GeneXpert MTB/RIF on BALF, isolation of drug-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis on liquid culture, and caseous necrosis with acid-fast bacilli on lung biopsy.
case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman with a history of metastatic cutaneous malignant melanoma—previously treated with high-dose interleukin-2 and subsequently receiving maintenance therapy with the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor pembrolizumab—presents with a one-week history of new-onset hemoptysis, expectorating approximately 10 mL of bloody sputum daily. She has experienced significant tumor regression under immunotherapy, though she has developed vitiligo, fatigue, mild oral ulceration, and dry mouth and eyes with positive anti-Ro52 autoantibodies. She reports no fever, chills, night sweats, cough, or weight loss.

On physical examination, she is afebrile with normal vital signs. Chest auscultation reveals clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes or crackles. There is no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Cutaneous examination reveals vitiliginous patches and two small, residual regressed pigmented macules on the left plantar foot.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals peripheral blood CD4+ and CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts above normal limits (1,544/μL and 712/μL, respectively); routine hematology and biochemical panels are otherwise unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest demonstrates interval enlargement of a preexisting solitary nodular opacity located in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe of the lung, with no associated mediastinal lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In a patient with metastatic melanoma, an enlarging pulmonary nodule associated with hemoptysis strongly suggested progressive metastatic disease; however, transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated extensive caseous necrosis without malignant melanocytic cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The chest CT (Figure 1C) showed the increased size of the lesion in the right upper lobe without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Immune-Related Adverse Event / Checkpoint Inhibitor Pneumonitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The patient had well-documented immune-related adverse events from pembrolizumab (sicca syndrome, vitiligo, positive anti-RO52 antibodies), raising consideration for autoimmune pneumonitis; however, chest CT revealed a localized expanding upper lobe lesion rather than diffuse interstitial/ground-glass opacities, and microbiologic testing confirmed mycobacteria.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Nevertheless, the patient developed fatigue and dry mouth and skin, raising suspicion of Sjogren's syndrome with a positive concentration of the autoimmune antibody RO52 in the peripheral blood test.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis activated during PD-1 inhibition
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Unconcentrated bronchoalveolar lavage fluid tested positive on GeneXpert MTB/RIF without rifampin resistance mutations, liquid culture isolated drug-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and transbronchial biopsy demonstrated abundant caseous necrosis with acid-fast bacilli.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Unconcentrated BALF was tested positive for GeneXpert Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB)/RIF with low semi-quantitative value. Additionally, mutations in rpoB gene that confer rifampicin resistance were not detected. The liquid culture and drug sensitivity test for BALF indicated MTB to be drug sensitive. Both examinations confirmed the diagnosis of active pulmonary TB. The transbronchial lung biopsy specimen showed a large amount of caseous necrosis (Figure 2A and B) with mediate lymphocyte infiltrate but few acid-fast bacilli.

editor_comments: Distilled following Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission prompt captures the oncologic background (PD-1 inhibition), new hemoptysis, and chest CT showing the enlarging right upper lobe nodule while strictly omitting bronchoscopy, GeneXpert, biopsies, and pathogen names. Diagnostic reasoning details the critical discrimination between melanoma metastasis, autoimmune pneumonitis, and activated tuberculosis.
